source.title: Who Saves and Why
source.summary: Time preference, the lifecycle hypothesis, and the wahn thesis: how akhirah-oriented preferences could change savings behavior fundamentally.
source.author: Islamic Economics
source.body_text: The Solow model says the savings rate determines the steady state. Higher savings means more capital accumulation and higher output per worker. So what determines how much people save? Standard economics offers the lifecycle hypothesis and permanent income hypothesis, both assuming a particular discount rate. The wahn thesis asks: what if the discount rate is endogenous? If an agent genuinely believes in akhirah, their effective planning horizon extends beyond death. They're not smoothing consumption over 80 years but optimizing over an infinite horizon. This changes savings behavior, charitable giving, and investment allocation simultaneously. The net effect on measured savings is ambiguous, but the allocation should be more efficient. This is theoretically interesting but empirically unproven, and this episode says so honestly.
